parts.text: computeVisibleItems uses measuredHeights but how does horizontal still works without changing that function measuredWidths?

Because `computeVisibleItems` never measures anything — it only does arithmetic on numbers, and the *axis of those numbers is decided at the measurement boundaries*, which are exactly the seams the subclass overrides.

Follow the data flow:

**Who writes `measuredHeights`:**
- `VirtualScrollerItem` with `axis="x"` captures `getBoundingClientRect().width` and emits it → `syncItemHeight(index, width)` stores it.
- `remeasureRenderedItems` reads each rendered element through `this.rectSize(el)` — overridden to return the rect's **width**.

So in a horizontal instance, the map named `measuredHeights` *contains widths*. The map is just `Record<index, number>` — "measured main-axis size per item"; nothing in its storage or the cursor bookkeeping knows or cares which axis the pixels came from.

**Who reads it — `computeVisibleItems`:** pure prefix-sum arithmetic. It walks `cursor.offset += measured[i] ?? assumed` against two other numbers: `scrollTop` (parsed from `scrollPosition`, which the horizontal class fills with the X offset — lenis targets, `setScrollPosition`, the whole scroll pipeline is axis-blind numbers) and `this.containerHeight.value` — a *getter*, overridden in the subclass to return `elementSize.width`. Sum sizes until you cover the viewport extent, pad, emit spacer sizes. At no point does the function touch the DOM or an axis-specific API. Same story for `scrollHeight`, `getIndexPosition`, `getIndexAtPosition`, the snap, the seek/converge loop — they're all "offsets and extents along the scroll axis."

That was the whole point of the seam design: the hand-tuned 80% (cursor math, render-bias rebasing, windowing, creep, converge) operates on *main-axis quantities* and never forks; only the six places that translate between DOM/gesture reality and those quantities (`rectSize`, `offsetSize`, `transformFor`, `axisPaddingProps`, `axisDelta`, the lenis orientation options) plus the two container-size getters know which axis they're on. Ten overrides, zero duplicated math.

The honest cost you've spotted: the **names now lie** in the horizontal reading — `measuredHeights` holding widths, `containerHeight` returning a width, `scrollHeight` meaning "scroll extent." They're vertical-flavored names for axis-neutral quantities, kept because renaming would churn the tuned file. If you want, I can do the pure-rename pass (`measuredHeights → measuredSizes`, `containerHeight → containerSize`, `scrollHeight → scrollExtent`, `syncItemHeight → syncItemSize`, etc.) — mechanical, no behavior change, and the public API surface (`assumedHeight` prop included) is the one decision point since consumers touch it.

parts.text:
Switched and committed (dd66e97). The vocabulary now matches the semantics your question exposed:

| was (vertical-flavored) | now (axis-neutral) |
|---|---|
| `measuredHeights` | `measuredSizes` |
| `assumedHeight` / `:assumed-height` | `assumedSize` / `:assumed-size` |
| `containerHeight` / `containerOuterHeight` | `containerSize` / `containerOuterSize` |
| `scrollHeight` (class getter) | `scrollExtent` |
| `syncItemHeight` / `computeScrollHeight` | `syncItemSize` / `computeScrollExtent` |
| `estimatedItemHeight`, spacer `…Height`s | `estimatedItemSize`, spacer `…Size`s |

So `computeVisibleItems` now *reads* as what it always *was*: prefix sums of main-axis sizes against a scroll offset and a container extent — and the horizontal subclass's overrides (`containerSize` → width, `rectSize` → width) stop looking like tricks and start looking like the design.

Scope held deliberately tight: the scroller family, every live consumer (archive rail, drip showcase, docs example wrapper), and the docs/blog pages that document the API (`virtual-scroller.md`, the million-rows post, derivations-are-free) — so no published page teaches a dead prop name. The vendored lenis keeps `scrollHeight` (there it means the DOM concept), and the legacy `demo/` copy stays its own self-consistent vintage.

Two bonuses from the pass: `ignoreNativeScroll` is now a properly typed `LenisOptions` field (the `as any` casts are gone), which also returned the playground's tsc count to its exact 46-error baseline — the rename itself added zero. Measured right now on this machine (repo's Vue 3.5, Node 26, 100k allocations, forced GC deltas):

| cell | bytes/instance |
|---|---|
| `ref(number)` | **160** |
| `shallowRef(number)` | **160** |
| `computed` (never read) | **320** |
| `computed` (read once) | **320** |
| `computed` + a live subscriber | **633** (includes the effect object itself) |

So yes — **a ref is half a computed**, and the docs' "~300 bytes" computed claim reproduces (320 here). The reason for the 2× is structural: a `RefImpl` is only a *dependency* (value + one `Dep`), while a `ComputedRefImpl` is both a dependency *and a subscriber* — it carries the getter closure, its own dep-link list to everything it reads, dirtiness/version bookkeeping, plus the same outbound `Dep`. It's two roles in one object. And note `computed` pays its 320 at *allocation*, before anyone reads it — which is exactly why the Standard demands a stated reason before allocating one.

On the scroller — your instinct is right, but the lightweight story is even better than "only 2 computeds," because the count that matters is **per item, and it's zero**:

- **Per instance** (one per rail/strip): ~13 refs + 2 computeds ≈ 13×160 + 2×320 ≈ **2.7 KB of reactive machinery, total** — and there's one instance, so this is noise.
- **Per item**: no ref, no computed, no proxy, no wrapper. An item's entire footprint in the scroller is *one number in a plain record* (`measuredSizes[index]`) — and only after it has actually been rendered once. A 100k-item list you never scroll costs the scroller a length read; memory grows with how far you've *read*, not how much *exists*. That plus the O(1) aggregates and the cursor is the whole state.
- **The derivations are free tier at work**: `leadingSpacerPx`, `trailingSpacerPx`, the scrollbar fractions, `estimatedItemSize` — all plain getters, 0 bytes each. In ordinary composition style most of those would reflexively be `computed`s "for safety": eight more cells ≈ 2.5 KB *plus subscriber links*. Here the two computeds that exist (`visibleItems`, `scrollExtent`) are surgical — both justified as caching shells over hot recomputation, both O(window) inside.

So the honest summary: the scroller is lightweight not because 2 < 8, but because its cost model is **O(items-ever-rendered) numbers + O(1) cells**, while the naïve virtual list is O(items) reactive objects. That's the "reactivity is an allocator" thesis running in production.

If you want, these ref/computed numbers are one `measure:` script away from joining the memory table in `performance.md` — the 160/320 pair would slot nicely next to the existing per-derivation rows. Say the word.

Exactly right on all three counts.

On the mechanism: a ref only has to answer "who's watching me" — one `Dep`, one outbound edge list. A computed additionally has to answer "what am I watching, is any of it stale, and at which version did I last compute" — the inbound link list, dirtiness flags, version counters, the closure. Half the roles, half the bytes.

On the docs: agreed, nothing to write — `ref()` in an ivue class *is* Vue's ref, byte for byte. That's the point the state page now makes explicitly: ivue decides where the refs live, never what they are. A number ivue didn't cause doesn't belong in ivue's memory table.

And the attribution is the honest one, worth keeping crisp because it's the stronger claim for both sides: **ivue set the price list, the design did the shopping.** ivue's contribution is that plain getters cost zero and `computed` is opt-in with a stated reason — so the *default* path never taxes you. But nothing in ivue forced the decisions that make the scroller what it is: one number per rendered item instead of a cell per item, the movable prefix-sum cursor instead of a materialized positions array, geometry invalidation as a single version bump, snapshot-compare so a stable window re-renders nothing, the render-bias rebase. Those are algorithmic choices that would be just as good ideas in any framework — ivue's role was to not punish them, and to keep them readable as named members on one prototype instead of a closure tangle. A cheap allocator plus a design that barely allocates: that's the compounding, and it's the same story the 20M-cell grid tells.

i was wondering to use this lightweightness to make even marque like inline text scroll, for long texts to show even books as one line that's scrolling, and even have a lot of em, feasible?

Feasible — and almost embarrassingly so, because the two hard problems a "book as one scrolling line" poses are the two problems the scroller has already solved at larger scale than you'd need.

**The mapping is direct.** A book becomes items by chunking at whitespace (say 8–12 words per chunk, `white-space: pre` so trailing spaces render and measure): a 600k-character book ≈ 8–10k chunks — a tenth of the 100k items the vertical scroller is proven at. Each chunk's entire cost is one number in `measuredSizes`, and only after it first scrolls into view. The DOM at any moment is ~15–30 spans regardless of book length. Total virtual extent ≈ 4–5M px — well under the ~10M px posts the render-bias rebasing was built for, and `renderBias` is already axis-neutral (it flows through `transformFor`), so f32 compositor precision holds at chapter 40 exactly as it does at page one.

**The marquee motion already exists and is the best part.** The reading creep — the per-frame fractional integrator with the compositor-glide delivery that got hand-tuned against judder — *is* a marquee engine. It lives in the base class, writes through the axis seams, and pauses/resumes around user input. A marquee is the creep at a chosen `CREEP_MS_PER_PX` (probably a speed prop rather than the constant). And you get behaviors no CSS marquee has: the reader can grab the line, scrub backward with lenis physics, release, and the crawl resumes; seek-to-fraction gives you "jump to chapter 12" on a one-line book.

**Many at once** is the only place with a real budget: each instance is ~2.7 KB of reactive cells plus one rAF loop *while creeping*. With the IntersectionObserver gating the archive rail already uses (offscreen ⇒ no rAF), **dozens on a page are trivial**. Hundreds simultaneously visible would want a shared frame pump (one rAF driving all creeps) and arguably a lenis-free mode — a pure marquee doesn't need wheel physics, and Lenis is the heaviest per-instance piece. Both are small, additive extensions; neither is needed for the first version.

Two genuinely new bits to build, both small: a `chunkText()` that splits on whitespace and pre-estimates widths via canvas `measureText` (font metrics are stable, so `assumedSize` calibration would be near-exact from the start — fewer measurement corrections than the blog posts ever had); and, if you want the classic infinite loop rather than reach-the-end behavior, a seamless wrap mode (modular position) — the current `autoRepeat` resets to start with a pause, which is right for a *book* (it's a reader wearing a marquee costume, not a loop).

So: a `TextMarquee`/`BookLine` component is mostly a *consumer* of what exists — chunker + `HorizontalVirtualScroller` + creep-on-visible. It would also make a killer playground example and blog post ("a whole book in one line — 30 DOM nodes"). Want me to build it?

Good instincts all three — let me take them in order, because they interlock nicely.

**1. Purity boundary: fully agreed, and it's cheap to keep.** The scroller's vocabulary stays *items, sizes, pixels* — it never learns what text is. The only change it needs for the marquee is one **generic** knob it arguably should have had anyway: creep speed is currently a hard static (`CREEP_MS_PER_PX = 150`). An optional `creepMsPerPx` prop with the static as fallback keeps the tuned default sacred while making speed a setting — that's a scroll-domain concept, so it belongs in the scroller. Everything else lands in two new pieces:

```
TextChunker      — Static() class, pure: text → chunks (whitespace-safe),
                   canvas measureText pre-estimation. Knows nothing of scrolling.
TextMarquee      — Reactive() class: owns text/speed/play state, composes
                   TextChunker output into scroller items. Knows nothing of fonts' internals
                   or prefix sums.
HorizontalVirtualScroller — untouched except the speed prop.
```

**2. ivue classes everywhere — agreed, and there's an admission to make:** `BlogDripShowcase.vue` currently violates our own Standard — refs, an interval, free functions, all naked in script setup. `script_setup_is_wiring_only` would flag it if the docs theme were gated. Same for the scrollbar drag handlers sitting as free functions in `VirtualScroller.vue`'s setup. The plan converts the showcase to a proper `$DripShowcase` class (and I'd fold the scrollbar handlers into the scroller class in the same pass); the marquee is born conformant. Our flagship home component should survive our own gate.

**3. Props inside the namespace — I think you've found a real deepening of the pattern, and I'd go further than "should we":** the namespace already *is* the component's manifest (`$Class`, `Class`, `Instance`); props and emits are the rest of the same contract. Concretely:

```ts
export namespace VirtualScroller {
  export const $Class = $VirtualScroller;
  export let Class = Reactive($Class) as unknown as typeof $VirtualScroller;
  export type Instance<T extends BaseItem> = ReactiveInstance<$VirtualScroller<T>>;

  // the component contract, runtime + type, defaults included
  export const props = {
    modelValue: { type: Array as PropType<BaseItem[]>, required: true },
    assumedSize: { type: Number, default: 30 },
    snapToItems: { type: Boolean, default: false },
    creepMsPerPx: { type: Number, default: undefined },
    /* … */
  } as const;
  export type Props<T extends BaseItem> = VirtualScrollerProps<T>; // the generic face
}
```

The SFC becomes pure wiring: `const props = defineProps(VirtualScroller.props) as unknown as VirtualScroller.Props<T>` — runtime object for Vue, generic interface for TS. And the horizontal variant expresses its differences the same way a house gate does: `HorizontalVirtualScroller.props = { ...VirtualScroller.props, assumedSize: { type: Number, default: 300 } }`.

Three concrete wins beyond aesthetics:

- **It kills a live bug-shaped duplication**: today both SFCs repeat the whole `withDefaults` block, and they've already drifted (`assumedSize: 30` vs `300` — semantic, but *implicit*; spread-with-override makes it a visible one-line ruling).
- **It retires the deploy failure class entirely**: runtime props objects need no compiler-sfc *type* resolution, so cross-file imports stop requiring `typescript` in the building project. The dep we added stays as belt-and-suspenders, but the trap is gone by construction.
- **It's the extensible-components idea landed in its right home** — the choose-field pattern already proved props-as-runtime-objects for extension; moving them into the namespace unifies it with the class manifest instead of a parallel `*Props.ts` convention. (The `before--`/`after--` slot forwarding half of that pattern I'd *not* adopt here — the scroller has one slot; that machinery earns nothing.)

One honest limitation to accept: with runtime props, prop types in the template come through the cast rather than compiler magic — for a generic component that's what we already do (`generic="T"` + cast), so nothing is lost, but it's worth saying the compile-time-destructure-defaults style becomes unavailable (we don't use it anyway). And one deliberate *non*-step for now: I would **not** add a gate check ("props live in the namespace") until the pattern has survived a couple of components — same discipline as every other Standard evolution this week: prove it, then legislate it.

**Proposed build order** (each verifiable alone): ① namespace-props refactor on both scroller SFCs + `creepMsPerPx` seam; ② `BlogDripShowcase` → class (+ scrollbar handlers into the scroller class); ③ `TextChunker` + `TextMarquee` + playground example with a genuinely long text, speed slider in the demo; ④ drive it live, then the docs example page.

1	---
2	title: Extensible Components
3	description: 'Classes extend — so props, emits and slots must extend with them. The params/defaults architecture: typed props + plain defaults merged by propsWithDefaults(), ExtractEmitTypes for emits, ExtendSlots for wrappable slots.'
4	relatedPosts: [the-options-api-everyone-wanted, inheritance-exile]
5	---
6	
7	# Extensible Components
8	
9	ivue components are classes, and classes extend. A `ContactField` that
10	extends the choose-field machinery needs its **entire surface** to extend
11	with it — props inherited, re-defaulted and grown; emits carried through;
12	slots wrappable rather than replaced.
13	Vue's `withDefaults(defineProps<T>())` macro cannot express that: its
14	defaults are locked inside a compiler transform, invisible to any wrapper.
15	
16	This page describes the **params/defaults architecture** the advanced
17	field components use: every prop declared once as a type, every default
18	declared once as a plain value, and `propsWithDefaults()` merging them
19	into a standard Vue props object — one that a child component can spread,
20	re-default, and grow.
21	
22	## The shape
23	
24	Three declarations per component, each doing exactly one job:
25	
26	```ts
27	// ChooseFieldProps.ts (excerpt)
28	import type { ExtractPropTypes, PropType } from 'vue';
29	import {
30	  propsWithDefaults,
31	  type ExtractEmitTypes,
32	  type ExtractPropDefaultTypes,
33	} from 'ivue';
34	
35	/** 1 — the TYPES: a defineComponent-style object, no defaults inside. */
36	export const chooseFieldParamsTypes = {
37	  multiple: { type: Boolean as PropType<boolean> },
38	  useChips: { type: Boolean as PropType<boolean> },
39	  inputDebounce: { type: Number as PropType<number> },
40	  fetchPath: { type: String as PropType<string> },
41	  fetchRowsPerPage: { type: Number as PropType<number> },
42	  optionLabelPriority: { type: Array as PropType<string[]> },
43	};
44	
45	/** 2 — the DEFAULTS: plain values, typed against the types object. */
46	export const chooseFieldParamsDefaults: ExtractPropDefaultTypes<
47	  typeof chooseFieldParamsTypes
48	> = {
49	  multiple: false,
50	  useChips: false,
51	  inputDebounce: 250,
52	  fetchPath: '',
53	  fetchRowsPerPage: 20,
54	  optionLabelPriority: ['label', 'name', 'value', 'id'],
55	};
56	
57	/** 3 — the MERGE: a standard Vue props object, ready for defineProps. */
58	export const chooseFieldProps = propsWithDefaults(
59	  chooseFieldParamsDefaults,
60	  chooseFieldParamsTypes,
61	);
62	export type IChooseFieldProps = ExtractPropTypes<typeof chooseFieldProps>;
63	```
64	
65	## Extension is the point
66	
67	Because the types and defaults are plain, inspectable objects, a wrapping
68	component composes its props surface by spread — inherit everything,
69	override the defaults that define its specialization, add its own:
70	
71	```ts
72	// ContactFieldProps.ts — extends the choose-field surface
73	export const contactFieldParamsTypes = {
74	  ...chooseFieldParamsTypes,
75	  /** Compact display mode: smaller avatar, name only, denser rows. */
76	  compact: { type: Boolean as PropType<boolean> },
77	};
78	
79	export const contactFieldParamsDefaults: ExtractPropDefaultTypes<
80	  typeof contactFieldParamsTypes
81	> = {
82	  ...chooseFieldParamsDefaults,
83	  fetchPath: '/contact',                              // its endpoint
84	  optionLabelPriority: ['name', 'email', 'id'],       // its label rules
85	  optionDescriptionPriority: ['role', 'company'],     // its captions
86	  compact: false,                                     // its own prop
87	};
88	
89	export const contactFieldParams = propsWithDefaults(
90	  contactFieldParamsDefaults,
91	  contactFieldParamsTypes,
92	);
93	```
94	
95	This is the props-side mirror of `class $ContactField extends
96	ChooseField.$Class` — the class hierarchy and the props hierarchy extend
97	together. See it live in the
98	[Advanced Select Field example](/examples/choose-field), where
99	`ContactField` is exactly this wrapper.
100	
101	`propsWithDefaults` is **non-mutating** by design: spreading a types map
102	shares the inner `{ type }` descriptor objects, so an in-place
103	implementation would silently rewrite the base component's defaults when
104	the child applies different ones. Each descriptor is copied — the base
105	surface is never touched by its children.
106	
107	## Why not `withDefaults(defineProps<T>())`?
108	
109	Vue's macro form is right for small, terminal components. It stops
110	scaling exactly where extensible components begin:
111	
112	- **Macro defaults aren't data.** They're locked inside a compiler
113	  transform — a wrapper cannot import them, spread them, or override
114	  three of them.
115	- **Object and array defaults become factory noise.** In the macro form
116	  every non-primitive default must be a function. `propsWithDefaults`
117	  handles it once: objects and arrays are wrapped in cloning factories
118	  automatically (via `structuredClone`; pass a custom cloner for exotic
119	  values), primitives pass through untouched.
120	- **`ExtractPropDefaultTypes` keeps the pair honest**: the defaults object
121	  must provide a correctly-typed value for every declared type, so a new
122	  prop without a default is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.
123	
124	## Emits and slots, same discipline
125	
126	Emits are declared as an object of validators and converted to the emit
127	function's type by `ExtractEmitTypes`; slots interfaces extend a wrapped
128	component's slots with `before--`/`after--` prefixed variants via
129	`ExtendSlots`, which is what lets a wrapping component inject content
130	around every inherited slot without redeclaring any of them:
131	
132	```ts
133	export const chooseFieldEmits = {
134	  'update:model-value': (newValue: any) => true,
135	  remove: (removed: { index: number; value: any }) => true,
136	};
137	export type IChooseFieldEmits = ExtractEmitTypes<typeof chooseFieldEmits>;
138	```

input.new_string: ## What to notice - **Rows in the DOM** stays at the window size while you fly through 1,000,000 items — watch the counter while scrolling. - **Jumps converge.** A jump lands on an estimated position, then re-applies as the fresh window measures in — watch the landing settle onto row #500,000. - **The scrollbar is code.** `overflow-anchor: none` and a `translateZ` compositor layer keep the browser out of the way; Lenis takes its clamp from the computed content height, not the DOM. ## The contract lives in the namespace The scroller's namespace carries the **whole component contract**, not just the class: prop types, prop defaults, the merged runtime props object, emits, slots and the expose-surface type. The SFC is pure wiring against it — ```ts const props = defineProps( VirtualScroller.props ) as unknown as VirtualScroller.Props; const emit = defineEmits(VirtualScroller.emits) as VirtualScroller.Emits; ``` `defineProps` receives a plain **runtime object** (types and defaults merged by [`propsWithDefaults`](/guide/extensible-components)), so the compiler never resolves a cross-file type inside a macro, and the cast recovers the generic `` precision a runtime map cannot carry. The payoff is the same one the class hierarchy already has: a subclass component composes its surface by **spread**. `HorizontalVirtualScroller` — the same tuned class rotated sideways through its axis seams — inherits every prop and states its one real difference in one line: ```ts export const propsDefaults = { ...VirtualScroller.propsDefaults, assumedSize: 300 // cards are ~hundreds of px wide where rows are tens tall }; ``` ## A book as one scrolling line The same machinery, pointed at text: a **marquee** that scrolls a ~400,000-character book as a single unbroken line. Three units, each pure about one thing: - **`TextChunker`** (a plain static class) speaks only text: it collapses the book to one line, cuts it into ~400-character chunks at spaces so words never split — each chunk keeping its trailing space, so side by side they concatenate back byte-identically — and canvas-measures the font's average character width. - **`HorizontalVirtualScroller`** speaks only items, sizes and pixels. It never learns it is scrolling a book. - **`TextMarquee`** is where they meet: chunks become items, the measured character width seeds `assumed-size`, and the glide is the scroller's own autoplay creep — the per-frame integrator that paces article reading — with its speed exposed through the `creep-ms-per-px` prop. ## Kill your test servers — the CPU-cap incident

A session left running at once: two `wrangler dev` instances (workerd +
miniflare + esbuild watchers EACH), an `npx serve`, and an orphaned
headless Chromium (a Playwright script threw after launch, so
`browser.close()` never ran — node exits on uncaught rejection and the
browser survives as an orphan). Together they capped the VM's CPUs and
forced a reboot.

Rules: one dev server at a time, kill by port when done
(`kill $(lsof -t -i:PORT)`); wrap Playwright drives in try/finally so
the browser closes on error; before ending any session that started
background processes, sweep:
`ps aux | grep -E "wrangler|workerd|serve|chrom" | grep -v grep`.

- **VitePress intercepts link clicks on `window` in the CAPTURE phase** (`router.js`): it runs before any element handler, so `event.preventDefault()` / `stopPropagation()` in a Vue `@click` are too late — the router still `go(href)`s, and a `history.go(-n)` you fire afterwards walks back from the NEW entry (symptom: wrong page + history length grows by one). To own a click on an internal `<a>`, put `vp-raw` on the anchor (the router skips `.closest(".vp-raw")`), or use a `<button>` (it skips `closest("button")` too). `BlogBackLink.vue` is the reference.

- **Never patch a large generated/authored TS file with ad-hoc sed/python splices** — two rounds of "replace this block" scripts left `check-standard.ts` with duplicated regions and phantom syntax errors that cost more than the file was worth. When a multi-hundred-line file needs structural surgery, truncate and re-Write it whole from the known-good content; `Edit` with unique anchors for small changes only. Corollary: a script that computes slice indices must assert `findIndex !== -1` before slicing — a `-1` fed to `slice(end+1)` silently duplicates the whole file.

- **Bun exits before draining microtasks scheduled from a `beforeExit` handler** — a `process.once('beforeExit', () => main().then(code => process.exit(code)))` bootstrap loses the exit code under Bun: the process exits 0 before the `.then` runs, so every refusal reports success (the purest silent-instrument failure — CI green forever). Node drains those microtasks; Bun 1.4 does not. Fix: hold the loop open with a `setInterval` keep-alive until `main` resolves, then `clearInterval` + `process.exit(code)`. Applies to every deferred-main CLI bootstrap (ivue-standards-check.ts, invariants-check.ts); ALWAYS verify a CLI's nonzero exit paths with `cmd >/dev/null 2>&1; echo $?` — piping through `tail` reports the pipe's exit, not the command's, which is how this hid twice.

- **Lenis adopts native scroll on animation COMPLETE, not just on native scroll events** — `reset()` (called when a lerp finishes) sets `targetScroll = actualScroll`, and in a fully-virtual scroller the wrapper's native scrollLeft/scrollTop is pinned 0, so the first completed wheel lerp teleports the content back to origin. The vertical scroller never hit it in years because its autoplay creep re-targets before any lerp completes. Fix: `ignoreNativeScroll` option in the fork (reset keeps `animatedScroll`; onNativeScroll returns early) — and remember the fork's constructor DESTRUCTURES options: an unknown key silently vanishes (`lenis.options.myFlag === undefined` is the tell). Debug technique that found it: `Object.defineProperty(lenis, 'targetScroll', {set(v){log(stack)}})` — watch the mutation, not the symptom.

# Shared FramePump — one rAF scheduler for N animating scrollers

**Status:** designed, deliberately deferred.
**Trigger:** dozens of concurrently ANIMATING scroller/marquee instances
on one page (a wall-of-marquees demo, a post player with many
auto-creeping strips). Today's worst page runs 2–3 rAF loops — below the
threshold, so building now is unproven labor.

## What it is

A `Static()` class (`FramePump`) holding a registry of animating
instances. Instances register while animating and unregister when
settled; the pump runs ONE `requestAnimationFrame` loop while the
registry is non-empty and stops when it empties. One pump per app,
statics read through `self` — the shared-store Static pattern
coordinating N `Reactive` instances.

## What it buys (in order of weight)

1. **Read/write phasing — the real argument.** Each scroller's frame
   path both writes (transform, spacer sizes) and reads layout
   (`offsetSize` in the clamp). Spacer writes dirty layout, so N
   instances animating in the same tick can interleave
   write → read → write → read: up to N forced layouts per frame.
   A coordinator runs the two-phase schedule — ALL reads, then ALL
   writes — collapsing that to at most one layout per frame regardless
   of N. Independent rAF loops structurally cannot do this.
2. **Lifecycle.** Offscreen instances (IntersectionObserver) don't tick;
   "who deserves a frame" is decided in one place instead of N little
   state machines.
3. **Budgeting/priority.** The visible marquee gets full cadence,
   below-fold strips half rate — and the pump composes with the
   ParagraphMeasurer idle pump (see paragraph-measurer.md): one
   scheduler owning the frame budget for animation AND measurement.

## What it does NOT buy

Frames. The browser already coalesces every rAF callback into one vsync
tick with one timestamp — ten loops ≠ ten frames, and clock consistency
already exists. Per-frame scheduling overhead of N registrations is
tiny. Do not sell the pump as "fewer frames"; sell it as phasing +
lifecycle + budget.

## Migration seams (already in place — no debt accruing by waiting)

The per-frame work already lives behind narrow methods on
`$VirtualScroller`: `creepStep` (autoplay integrator) and `loop` (lenis
raf while wheel-scrolling). Migration = instances hand those to the
registry instead of arming their own rAF. No redesign.

# ParagraphMeasurer — exact vertical sizes from the layout oracle

**Status:** designed AND benchmarked (2026-08-28, Parallels VM, headless
Chromium — real desktops faster). Target: the post player (100k-paragraph
posts); optionally a docs book-reader example first.
**Ruling:** tier 3 only. The prediction tiers (canvas line-count
estimate; unique-word-cache wrap simulation) stay UNBUILT — at these
costs they are dead labor. Invariant: *the engine that renders is the
only oracle of its own layout — never simulate the oracle when asking it
is cheap enough.* (The marquee's `measureText` obeys the same rule: for
a single unwrapped line, canvas IS the engine's answer — proven 0.1px.)

## The device

Pure `Static()` class: `(html[], context) → heights[]`. Internals:

- Hidden rig INSIDE the post's content element (inherits real font/CSS
  vars/width): `position: fixed; visibility: hidden` (never
  display:none — that skips layout), `contain: layout style`,
  explicit width. Containment is load-bearing: it isolates the rig's
  layout from the page's.
- **Write once, read many:** batch as one HTML string → `innerHTML` →
  read every `getBoundingClientRect().height`. First read forces THE
  layout; the rest are ~1µs clean reads.
- Images swapped for aspect-ratio-sized placeholder divs before
  injection (our content declares dimensions) — no network, no decode.
- `await document.fonts.ready` before measuring, or you measure the
  fallback font. (The marquee should gain this too.)
- Heights cached by `(post, width bucket, font)` — paragraphs don't
  change; reopen cost ~0ms. Width change invalidates; re-measure.

## Measured (scratchpad tier3-bench.html, realistic corpus: 25–115-word
paragraphs at 700px serif, ~8% with declared-dimension image blocks)

| corpus | strategy | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1,500 ¶ (normal book) | one synchronous batch | **27ms** total (~18µs/¶) — measure at open, before first paint |
| 100k ¶ (Mahabharata) | 20 × 5k batches | 1.94s total, worst batch 123ms |
| 100k ¶ | one giant batch | 1.89s — batching costs ~nothing |
| correctness | batched vs one-at-a-time forced layout | **max delta 0px** |

Cost is LINEAR (~18–19µs/¶ flat from 1.5k to 100k). Content height at
100k ≈ 15.1M px — inside the render-bias rebasing regime.

## Contention (10 books at once, rAF animation as victim)

| batch size (~slice) | frame p95 | frame max | dropped | wall (100k ¶ total) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5,000 ¶ (~100ms) | 100ms | 116ms | 20 + 1 stall | 1.85s |
| **1,000 ¶ (~20ms)** | **16.8ms** | **16.8ms** | **0** | **1.74s** |
| 500 / 250 ¶ | 16.8ms | 16.8ms | 0 | ~1.75s |

The finding that sets the design: `requestIdleCallback` only picks when
a slice STARTS — a 100ms slice still blocks whatever arrives mid-slice.
Unblocked means the SLICE fits the frame budget. And small batches cost
nothing (1.74s < 1.85s — better interleaving). So: one shared queue
across all books (no parallelism machinery — same thread anyway),
batches auto-tuned to ≤ ~10–15ms (time the first batch, halve until it
fits — self-calibrating for slow phones), first viewport of the open
book measured synchronously, the rest through the idle pump.

Tier-3 cannot run in a worker (no DOM there); `OffscreenCanvas`
measureText CAN — that shelf only reopens if a case ever demands full
extents synchronously without DOM access (SSR-ish). Not our case.

## Payoff in the player

With exact seeds the converge loop's reason to exist (landings drifting
as estimates refine) mostly evaporates; `seekToProgress` drags become
pixel-true on a 100k-paragraph post — same as proven on the book marquee
(end lands exactly at the opaque boundary).

# Ship the variant, keep the tuning

![Ship the variant, keep the tuning](/blog/ship-the-variant-keep-the-tuning.png)

<BlogPostDate />

Every codebase has one component that took years to get right. Ours is
a [virtual scroller](/examples/virtual-scroller) — a million rows, a
dozen divs, scroll physics driven by a customized Lenis instead of
native scroll. The feel is hand-tuned: a prefix-sum cursor that never
walks the whole list, a creep integrator that glides at fractional
pixels, origin rebasing that keeps the GPU in its precision comfort
zone. Call it the hard 80%.

Then you need it horizontal.

In most codebases that sentence starts a fork. Copy the file. Rename
it. Change every `height` to `width`, every `top` to `left`, every
`deltaY` to `deltaX`. Now there are two files, and every future fix
must remember to visit both. The fork is where tuning goes to rot.

Here is what the horizontal version actually cost:

```ts
class $HorizontalVirtualScroller<T> extends VirtualScroller.$Class<T> {
  protected get lenisOrientation() { return 'horizontal'; }
  protected get lenisGestureOrientation() { return 'horizontal'; }
  protected get lenisIgnoreNativeScroll() { return true; }
  protected offsetSize(el) { return el?.offsetWidth ?? 0; }
  protected rectSize(el) { return el.getBoundingClientRect().width; }
  protected transformFor(px) { return 'translateX(' + px + 'px)'; }
  protected get axisPaddingProps() { return ['padding-left', 'padding-right']; }
  protected axisDelta({ deltaX }) { return deltaX; }
}
```

Eight getters and methods. The cursor math, the render-bias rebasing,
the snap policy, the creep integrator, the seek-and-converge loop — the
tuned 80% — run unchanged, sideways.

> The hard part ships once. A variant pays only for its difference.

## Seams, not switches

The base class is an ivue class — ivue is a 1.1 kB class layer over
Vue's reactivity that lets components be plain classes. Plain classes
extend. That is the whole trick, but it only works if the base is
written for it.

The scroller touches the DOM's geometry in exactly eight places: which
dimension to read, which transform to write, which wheel delta to obey,
which paddings count toward the scroll extent. Each of those places is
a `protected` getter or method with the vertical answer as its body.
We call them axis seams.

The simple version: the scroller never says "height" directly. It asks
itself "how big is this, along my axis?" — and a subclass changes the
answer without touching the question.

A seam is not a mode flag. There is no `direction: 'horizontal'` prop
threading `if` branches through a thousand lines. The base class has
zero awareness that a horizontal variant exists. That is what keeps the
tuned code untouched: extension adds a layer, it never edits one.

One of the eight seams carries a behavior decision worth naming. The
horizontal strip obeys `deltaX` only — a plain vertical wheel passes
through to the page, and only a sideways gesture (shift+wheel, trackpad
swipe) drives the strip. A horizontal element that hijacks vertical
scrolling is how you make readers hate a page.

## The props inherit too

A component is not just its class. It is also its contract — props,
defaults, emits. If the class extends but the props are locked inside a
`withDefaults(defineProps<T>())` macro, the variant re-declares the
whole surface by hand, and the fork sneaks back in through the
front door.

… [74 characters removed from the sample] …

ace, and the variant composes it the way the class composes
behavior — by spreading and overriding:

```ts
export namespace HorizontalVirtualScroller {
  export const propsTypes = { ...VirtualScroller.propsTypes };
  export const propsDefaults = {
    ...VirtualScroller.propsDefaults,
    assumedSize: 300 // cards are hundreds of px wide; rows were tens tall
  };
  export const props = propsWithDefaults(propsDefaults, propsTypes);
}
```

Every prop inherited. One default overridden, with the reason on the
line. The SFC becomes pure wiring — `defineProps(X.props)` receives a
runtime object, and the resolved TypeScript type is derived from that
same object, never written twice. The full pattern is in the
[Extensible Components guide](/guide/extensible-components).

## The proof: a book as one scrolling line

Extension proves the seams. Composition proves the component. So we
pointed the horizontal scroller at something it was never built for: a
~400,000-character text, scrolling as a single unbroken line.

The scroller never learns it is scrolling a book. A separate
`TextChunker` — a pure static class, no reactivity — cuts the text into
~400-character chunks at word boundaries, each chunk keeping its
trailing space so side by side they concatenate back exactly. Chunks
become items. Items become five `<span>`s in the DOM at any moment,
because that is all the visible strip needs.

The numbers, measured with Playwright on a Linux VM (a slow
environment — your laptop does better): 401,789 characters, 1,010
chunks, 5 in the DOM, gliding at 120.0 ± 0.3 px/s on a 16.7 ms frame
cadence. The glide is the scroller's own autoplay creep — the same
integrator that paces article reading — with its speed exposed as a
prop. Drag the slider mid-glide and the speed changes without a
restart, because the integrator reads the live value every frame.

Two details came out sharper than expected:

**Exact sizes are cheap.** Virtual scrolling estimates the size of
unseen items, and estimates drift — ours ran about 1% small per chunk,
which compounds across a thousand chunks into a chunk and a half of
book hiding past the end of the scroll. The fix was not a better
estimate. `measureText` on a canvas returns the exact pixel width of an
unwrapped line, microseconds per chunk, and it matches the DOM to
0.1 px. The marquee measures every chunk up front and seeds the
scroller's size map. The end of the book now lands exactly at the edge
of the visible strip — verified to the pixel.

**Motion this smooth needs a transform, not a scrollbar.** Native
scrolling quantizes position to device pixels. The creep writes
fractional positions into a composited transform — at 120 px/s that is
two-ish pixels a frame, and the compositor filters the fractions into a
true constant-velocity glide. The same real-valued position model is
why a wheel flick hands off cleanly: the fling decays *to* cruise speed
and the creep adopts the scroll at that exact speed, mid-decay. It
never stalls to zero and restarts.

Here it is, running the shipped engine:

<ClientOnly>
  <ExampleTextMarquee />
</ClientOnly>

Shift+wheel scrubs it. The bar underneath drags — and lands where it
points, including the true end. A plain vertical wheel scrolls this
page, untouched.

## What this buys you

The vertical scroller shipped years of tuning. The horizontal strip
inherited all of it for eight overridden members. The marquee composed
the horizontal strip with a hundred lines of pure text machinery. Each
layer paid only for what it changed — and every fix to the base, past
and future, lands in all three.

That is the argument for classes as the unit of component authoring,
made with receipts instead of ideology. Composables share logic, but
they cannot take a *finished, tuned component* and produce a variant
that tracks the original. Extension can — when the component is a
class, its geometry passes through seams, and its contract is data.

> Write the hard 80% once. Let every variant subclass it.
